Shopify is great, but building your own stack gives you absolute freedom.

When we started STRAYED, everyone advised us to just set up a quick Shopify store and call it a day. It is the standard advice given to every new brand.

But we wanted to build something highly tailored, with a clean design aesthetic, zero restrictions and zero latency.

So we chose the harder path: custom MedusaJS, PostgreSQL, and an Oracle VPS.

It meant we had to manually configure server health monitors, handle database migrations, and build custom loyalty mechanics from scratch. But the reward is a site that loads instantly, has zero monthly subscription fees, and allows us to customize the entire checkout flow exactly how we want.

Bootstrapping means making conscious trade-offs between ease of setup and long-term control. For us, building from scratch was worth every single line of code.

Entering 1200 product variants manually into Odoo is a form of torture.

When we were setting up the inventory system for our brand, I thought I could just click through the Odoo UI. Ten minutes in, I realized that clicking through nested menus for every single color and size combination was going to take days.

My hands were literally cramping from the repetitive UI flow. But I didn't have the time to figure out another way.

But once I had time, I started figuring out how it works. It turns out Odoo is incredibly picky about column headers and relational IDs. One missing external ID in your CSV, and the whole import fails with a cryptic database error.

But once the formatting was perfectly aligned, importing 500 variants took less than ten seconds. Sometimes the best way to speed up your operations is to step back and build a proper data pipeline first, even if it feels like extra work upfront.

Cumulative Layout Shift was ruining our mobile shopping experience.

Our product images were jumping around the screen as the custom fonts loaded in. This layout shift was causing customers to accidentally click the wrong buttons during checkout.

To fix this, I set up font-display swap in our CSS and defined strict aspect-ratio boxes for all image containers. It seems like a minor thing, but stabilizing the layout improved our Core Web Vitals score dramatically.

We saw our mobile conversion rate improve slightly after fixing these layout shifts. It goes to show that good UX is not just about aesthetics, it is about keeping the layout stable while assets load.

I wasted six hours debugging a simple cache invalidation issue in our inventory view. 

We updated our product pricing in the database, but our frontend kept showing the old numbers for stale sessions. It turned out our Redis caching layer was set to a 24-hour TTL, which is way too long for a live retail store.

I ended up implementing a cache busting mechanism that triggers whenever an update mutation hits our MedusaJS backend. Now, the cache invalidates instantly upon change. It is funny how a single line of code regarding TTL settings can make your business look disorganized.

I spent three hours debugging a simple currency conversion rounding error last Tuesday.

We were showing prices on STRAYED with standard floating point math in JavaScript. It seemed fine until a customer pointed out that their cart total was off by exactly one paisa due to precision drift. That tiny error multiplied across thousands of transactions would have created a massive accounting nightmare.

I realized that using floats for money is a beginner mistake I should have avoided. I refactored the entire pricing module to use integer-based math by converting all prices to the smallest currency unit before performing any arithmetic.

It was a humbling reminder that the most basic concepts in computer science often cause the biggest headaches in production. When you are moving fast, it is incredibly easy to overlook the foundational rules that keep a financial system accurate.

It turned out the issue was much simpler and much more embarrassing. I had filled up the temporary disk space on my virtual machine because I was saving verbose debugging logs directly to the root directory during every test run. 

I cleaned up the logs and added a simple log rotation policy to the configuration file. The migrations run instantly now, and I saved myself from wasting even more time searching for a non-existent memory issue. 

Debugging is rarely about finding a sophisticated flaw in your logic. Most of the time, the solution is staring at you in the form of a full drive or a misconfigured environment variable.

I spent three days debugging a recursive shadow DOM issue in our custom checkout component. We were trying to inject a discount code field dynamically inside an iframe rendered by a payment provider. Every time the component re-rendered the script would lose reference to the parent state and cause the entire checkout page to lock up.

It was a classic case of trying to be too clever with our frontend architecture. I wanted the UI to feel completely native but that approach introduced a dependency chain that the browser simply was not designed to handle. I eventually had to strip out the custom injection and replace it with a standard overlay approach that hooks into the primary DOM tree instead.

Building your own stack means you have to deal with these browser-level limitations that pre-built platforms handle for you behind the scenes. You lose the ability to blame the provider for weird bugs but you gain total control over the UX. Sometimes the most frustrating bugs are just the cost of doing things your own way.
